title: Serving in hard places
tomorrow: what does an acrobat know about helping without burning out?

segments.voice: Yesterday, serving the earth: the bee's way, take lightly and leave things whole. Today, the places people tend to avoid.

Prisons, hospices, shelters: places you can drive past for years without going in. The leader of Mai's Thursday sit runs a meditation group at the county jail, and she asked if anyone could make simple art cards for the men there. Mai froze. Then Ava texted that her mom goes to the same jail with her church. In the suttas, the Buddha once walked straight down a road that farmers and travelers begged him not to take. On that road lived Angulimala, a killer feared across the king's land.
screen: `PLACES YOU DRIVE PAST.` → `ART CARDS FOR THE COUNTY JAIL.` → `THE ROAD EVERYONE AVOIDED.`

segments.voice: Angulimala sees a lone monk and runs after him with his sword. But however hard he runs, he can't catch the Buddha, who is only walking. Stop, monk! he shouts. The Buddha answers: I have stopped, Angulimala. You stop too. I've stopped harming living beings; you haven't. Something in Angulimala breaks open. He throws his weapons away and asks to become a monk. Later, on his alms round, people throw stones at him, and he bears it. That's the Buddhist answer to why anyone walks into hard places: the texts insist that even the man everyone fled can stop. Ava's family says something close in their own scripture. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says, in the King James words: "I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me." The shared part is real. Both send people toward the prisoner and the sick, not away from them. The difference is honest too. In Matthew, what's done for the least of these is done for Christ himself. In the Angulimala story, the weight falls on the one inside the hard place: he can stop, and wake up, through his own practice. Two reasons, one road toward the jail.
screen: `HE CAN'T CATCH A WALKING MONK.` · `"I HAVE STOPPED. YOU STOP TOO."` · `A NEIGHBOR: "I WAS IN PRISON…"` · `TWO REASONS, ONE ROAD.` · then, large: `HARD PLACES.`

segments.voice: Sit with your hands resting open on your knees, palms up, a posture with nothing to hide and nothing to defend. Bring to mind one hard place near you, a jail, a hospice, a shelter, and the people inside it tonight. Keep your hands open through the sit.
Serving in hard places: walking toward the places others avoid, because the texts say anyone there can stop and change.
Your line: hard places. Even the man everyone fled could stop. Twenty-four days, and one more road.

howItsDone: Buddhist volunteers and chaplains lead meditation groups in prisons, sit with the dying in hospices, and serve in shelters; the story of Angulimala is often told in that work as a sign that anyone can change.

notes: MN 86 paraphrased: cowherds and travelers warn the Buddha off the road; Angulimala pursues him but cannot catch him though the Buddha walks at an ordinary pace; 'I have stopped, Angulimala; you stop too' (the Buddha has laid aside the rod toward beings); Angulimala throws away his weapons and goes forth; later he is struck by thrown clods and stones on alms round and bears it. The finger-garland detail and any count of victims are left out on purpose. Confirm.
Parents: Angulimala is introduced as 'a killer'; no violence is described beyond the pursuit with a sword. Gentle enough for families; confirm.

Unity thread (wisdom day, and the monthly arc beat with Ava's family): Matthew 25:36 quoted from the KJV; 25:40 ('the least of these') paraphrased. Shared: going toward the prisoner and the sick. Difference: in Matthew, service to the least is service to Christ; in MN 86, the stress is on the person's own capacity to stop and awaken. Neither ranked; a Christian reviewer should confirm the framing.
